finding.claim: /fetch is guarded by is_safe_url, which resolves the hostname and rejects private, loopback, link-local and reserved addresses. The fetch then resolves the hostname again, so a DNS-rebinding attacker can return a public address to the check and an internal address (e.g. 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254) to the connection. This is the check-then-use pattern from case 12.

finding.sink: views.py:14 requests.get(url, timeout=5, allow_redirects=False) performs a fresh DNS lookup at connect time

finding.guards_checked: Scheme check (validators.py:12); hostname required (validators.py:12); IP class check on all getaddrinfo answers (validators.py:14-17); allow_redirects=False (views.py:14), which blocks redirect-based escape. Not guarded: DNS answer is not pinned between check and connect. Exploitability depends on the attacker controlling DNS with a short TTL, so severity is medium.

None of these is a closing guard under the rubric (no exact hostname allowlist, anchored match, or scheme plus strict host membership). allow_redirects=False at views.py:14 does not stop DNS rebinding. If the two disagree on the host (for example on backslashes, userinfo, or characters that urlparse strips), a URL that passes the check may connect to an internal host.
